passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a new dietary supplement on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults aged 40–60. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted with 100 participants, 50 assigned to the supplement group and 50 to a placebo. Baseline SBP was measured after an overnight fast, and participants were followed for 12 weeks. SBP was recorded at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks. The study aimed to determine whether the supplement could reduce SBP compared to placebo, and whether any reduction was clinically significant. The investigators also collected data on weight, heart rate, and adherence to the supplement regimen. Statistical analysis involved paired t-tests within groups and ANCOVA adjusting for baseline SBP and weight changes. The primary outcome was the mean change in SBP from baseline to 12 weeks.
stem: Which of the following best describes the study design used in this research?
explanation: The investigators randomly assigned participants to supplement or placebo groups and followed them prospectively, which is the hallmark of a randomized controlled trial.
trap: Choosing cohort study because participants were followed for 12 weeks; random assignment by the investigators makes it a randomized trial.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the passage and table?

options.A: Mean SBP fell more in the supplement group than in the placebo group.
options.B: The placebo group lost less weight than the supplement group.
options.C: Adherence was above 90% in the supplement group.

explanation: Correct: D) The passage describes the statistical methods but reports no test result or p-value, so statistical significance cannot be stated. Why the others are wrong: A) The supplement group fell 14 mmHg (138 to 124) versus 3 mmHg (139 to 136) for placebo. B) Placebo weight change was -0.5 kg versus -2.1 kg. C) Supplement adherence was 92%.
trap: Assuming the larger SBP fall means the difference was statistically significant; no p-value or test result is reported.

passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a new dietary supplement on systolic blood pressure (SBP) in adults aged 40–60. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) was conducted with 100 participants, 50 assigned to the supplement group and 50 to a placebo. Baseline SBP was measured after an overnight fast, and participants were followed for 12 weeks. SBP was recorded at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks. The study aimed to determine whether the supplement could reduce SBP compared to placebo, and whether any reduction was clinically significant. The investigators also collected data on weight, heart rate, and adherence to the supplement regimen. Statistical analysis involved paired t-tests within groups and ANCOVA adjusting for baseline SBP and weight changes. The primary outcome was the mean change in SBP from baseline to 12 weeks.
stem: How does the study’s design support the conclusion that the supplement lowered SBP?

options.A: Randomization reduces selection bias, and the placebo comparison accounts for changes that occur without the supplement.
options.B: The large sample size guarantees statistical significance.
options.C: The use of ANCOVA automatically proves causality.
options.D: The short follow-up period ensures immediate blood pressure changes.

explanation: Correct: A) Random assignment balances confounders across groups, and the placebo arm shows what happens without the supplement (139 to 136 mmHg). Why the others are wrong: B) No sample size guarantees significance; it depends on effect size and variability. C) ANCOVA adjusts for covariates but causal inference comes from the design, not the statistic. D) Follow-up length does not ensure any particular change in blood pressure.
trap: Believing a statistical technique or a large sample can by itself prove causality; causal inference rests on randomization and a comparison group.
